tldr: To prevent humanoid robots from toppling when lifting objects of unknown mass and shape, the authors developed a whole-body control framework that combines centroidal MPC, adaptive fuzzy compensation, and jerk-minimized optimal posture planning. They stably demonstrated lifting up to 10 kg payloads and walking while carrying loads on a real humanoid robot.
hero_caption: The complete material-handling sequence using the proposed method. Facing an unknown payload, the robot lowers its pelvis to crouch, stably lifts the box, walks while carrying it without losing balance, and finishes by placing it down. Adaptive fuzzy control instantly compensates for center-of-mass shifts, preventing falls.
overview:
For humanoid robots to handle materials in factories and warehouses designed for humans, they must stably lift and carry payloads. However, the mass and center of mass (CoM) of objects in real workplaces are rarely known in advance. Lifting an unexpectedly heavy payload drastically shifts the overall CoM of the robot. As a result, conventional model predictive control (MPC) alone can easily lose balance and fall.

To solve this, the authors did not try to estimate or identify payload mass and inertia online. Instead, they devised an adaptive fuzzy balance controller that applies corrective torques directly based on measurable balance deviations. They also combined this with an optimal posture planner that minimizes jerk while satisfying CoM stability constraints for smooth sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit transitions, integrating it all into a centroidal MPC whole-body control architecture.

In addition to validation in the MuJoCo physics simulator, they evaluated the framework on a real 28-DoF humanoid robot. While a conventional non-adaptive MPC toppled over with unknown payloads, the proposed method stably lifted 7 kg and 10 kg payloads. Furthermore, it demonstrated balance robustness by carrying a 7 kg payload during 15 seconds of walking and successfully placing it down.
contributions: Proposing a whole-body balancing framework that combines centroidal model predictive control (MPC) and adaptive fuzzy inference to compensate for CoM shifts under unknown loads without payload parameter identification.
Developing a smooth posture-transition planning method using a 3-link planar model and a triple-integrator that balances jerk minimization with CoM stability constraints.
Stably achieving the lifting of unknown payloads up to 10 kg and carrying a 7 kg payload while walking, verified in simulation and on a physical 28-DoF humanoid robot.

sections.heading: Three hurdles facing humanoid robots carrying unknown payloads
sections.summary: Lifting payloads is vital for humanoids working in human-centric environments, but unknown mass and CoM drastically alter robot dynamics. This paper solves this issue with a novel whole-body control framework integrating centroidal MPC, adaptive fuzzy compensation, and optimal posture-transition planning.
sections.details:
Humanoid robots mimic human anatomy, giving them great potential for flexible work in environments built for humans. In manufacturing and logistics, lifting and carrying tasks are in high demand. However, in real environments, the mass and inertia of payloads are not precisely known beforehand, posing an extreme challenge for robot control.

Specifically, three major bottlenecks exist:
- Dynamic instability from payload variations: Unknown mass and CoM cause the overall robot Center of Mass (CoM) to shift unexpectedly, easily leading to loss of balance.
- Posture transitions requiring complex whole-body coordination: Motions like crouching, grasping, and standing involve strong nonlinear dynamics and are hard to control smoothly.
- Lack of robustness against disturbances and contact forces: Controllers lack the flexibility to adapt to unknown external forces.

Building upon nonlinear MPC and whole-body control (WBC) based on centroidal dynamics, the authors propose a unified system. It combines an adaptive fuzzy balance controller that instantly compensates for unknown loads with a waypoint-based optimal posture planner that respects joint limits and stability. This achieves stable lifting and carrying without identifying payload parameters.

sections.heading: Why use fuzzy compensation instead of estimating payload weight?
sections.summary: Reviewing prior work on posture-transition optimization and fuzzy control, this section explains the design rationale for choosing fuzzy compensation over disturbance observers or online parameter identification. The goal is to retain MPC optimality while eliminating estimation delays and divergence risks.
sections.details:
### Challenges in Posture-Transition Trajectory Generation
In motion planning for sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit actions in humanoids, optimization methods using MPC and reduced-order models have advanced recently. However, most focus solely on walking locomotion or assume a constant payload mass. Real-time generation of smooth posture-transition trajectories while carrying unknown payloads has seen little progress.

### Why Fuzzy Control Instead of a Disturbance Observer?
When payload mass is unknown, classical methods often rely on disturbance observers (DOB), model reference adaptive control (MRAC), or online mass identification. However, the authors deliberately adopted a fuzzy compensator. When an unknown payload is added, the robot's mass, CoM position, and inertia tensor all change simultaneously. This mismatch is not a simple disturbance, but a complex state-dependent nonlinearity.

Online identification introduces computational convergence latency, making it impossible to keep up with sudden load changes at the moment of grasping. It also risks real-hardware divergence if adaptive gains become too large. In contrast, the proposed adaptive fuzzy controller directly outputs safe, saturated corrective moments based on rules using measurable Capture Point errors and CoM velocity. Bypassing mass identification loops provides strong transient response and ensures hardware safety—a major practical advantage.

sections.heading: Solving it hierarchically: Hybrid control with centroidal MPC and adaptive fuzzy inference
sections.summary: Centroidal MPC generates feasible reference motions and contact forces, which are converted to joint torques via inverse dynamics. A four-layer fuzzy inference system detects posture tilts caused by model mismatch via Capture Point error, distributing corrective torques directly to supporting-leg joints.
sections.details:
### Robot Model and Centroidal Dynamics
The robot's degrees of freedom are represented by floating base $\mathbf{q}_b \in SE(3)$ and joint angles $\mathbf{q}_j \in \mathbb{R}^{n_j}$, formulated via contact-constrained Euler-Lagrange equations. To reduce real-time computational burden, planning is reduced to a centroidal dynamics model using translational and angular momentum about the CoM, $\mathbf{h} = [\mathbf{h}_l^\top, \mathbf{h}_a^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{6}$.

### Whole-Body Tracking via Centroidal MPC and Inverse Dynamics
Solving a nonlinear MPC over a prediction horizon $T$ yields optimal CoM trajectories and contact wrenches satisfying friction cone and Center of Pressure (CoP) constraints. Instead of task-space quadratic programming (TS-QP), inverse dynamics is applied to the resulting desired accelerations and contact forces to compute joint torque commands. Because contact constraints and dynamic consistency are already handled by the higher-level nonlinear MPC, lower-level weight tuning and extra optimization are omitted, significantly slashing computational costs.

### Four-Layer Adaptive Fuzzy Inference System
To compensate for modeling errors caused by unknown payloads, the controller focuses on Capture Point (CP) deviations based on the linear inverted pendulum model. It takes three inputs: tracking error from the support polygon center $\mathbf{e}$, CoM velocity $\dot{\mathbf{r}}$, and accumulated error $\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{int}}$ to eliminate steady-state offsets.
The fuzzy inference system consists of four layers:
- Layer 1 (Fuzzification): Maps inputs to five linguistic variables (Negative Big, Negative Small, Zero, Positive Small, Positive Big) via Gaussian membership functions.
- Layer 2 (Rule Layer): Evaluates firing strengths across 125 rules formed by combinations of 3 inputs $\times$ 5 fuzzy sets.
- Layer 3 (Consequent Layer): Combines a PD-like base output with error integration effects.
- Layer 4 (Defuzzification): Computes corrective moments $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{comp}}^{\mathrm{task}}$ via weighted average and safely saturates them at predefined limits.

### Torque Distribution to Supporting Legs
The calculated corrective moments are distributed to supporting-leg joint torques rather than the upper body. Using the upper body for balance could disrupt hand grasp and drop the payload, so only the supporting leg joints compensate for CoM disturbances.

captions.F3: The proposed four-layer fuzzy inference system. It takes three inputs—Capture Point deviation, CoM velocity, and integrated error—and computes corrective pitch and roll torques through 125 rules. Because outputs are safely saturated, it avoids divergence on real hardware.

sections.heading: No jerky motions! Posture-transition planning with jerk minimization and CoM constraints
sections.summary: Crouching and standing motions for payload lifting are optimized using a 3-link planar model and a triple-integrator. This keeps joint jerk low for smooth motion while keeping the CoM within the support polygon throughout the trajectory.
sections.details:
### Smooth Trajectory Generation via Triple-Integrator
For bending and extending motions during lifting, a 3-link planar model consisting of hip, knee, and ankle joints ($\mathbf{q}_w = [q_h, q_k, q_a]^\top$) is used. To prevent shocks from rapid acceleration changes, a discrete-time triple-integrator model driven by jerk (the time derivative of acceleration) $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \dddot{\mathbf{q}}_w$ is adopted. This produces trajectories that are continuous and smooth in position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk.

### Pelvis Position Selection Algorithm and Inverse Kinematics
When given task commands for target pelvis height $h$ and target pitch angle $\theta$, infinitely many horizontal pelvis positions $p_x$ can keep the CoM within the support polygon. The proposed method introduces a selection algorithm that solves geometric inverse kinematics (using the law of cosines) to automatically find a feasible $p_x$ that satisfies joint limits and places the CoM inside the stable region.

### Constrained Optimization Formulation
A quadratic cost function is formulated and solved to minimize target joint tracking errors and jerk magnitude. Crucially, in addition to upper and lower bounds on joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk, an inequality stability constraint explicitly enforces that the CoM stays strictly within the support polygon across all time steps. This optimization generates smooth posture-transition trajectories without losing balance during rapid body posture changes.

captions.F4: The physical 28-DoF humanoid robot used in experiments (right) and the 3-link planar kinematic model used for posture-transition planning (left). Coordinated motions of the hip, knee, and ankle joints lower and raise the pelvis without compromising CoM stability.

sections.heading: Simulation and hardware tests: 10 kg lifting and load-carrying walking
sections.summary: The proposed method was evaluated in the MuJoCo simulator and on a real 28-DoF humanoid. While non-adaptive MPC pitched forward and fell under heavy loads, the proposed method kept a low posture to lift payloads stably and accomplished walking while carrying 7 kg.
sections.details:
### Control System Execution Rates and Hardware Setup
A life-sized humanoid robot with 28 degrees of freedom (7 DoF per arm, 6 DoF per leg) was used for validation. The control loop is multi-tiered: centroidal MPC generates reference motions at 50 Hz based on posture planning, the adaptive framework computes joint torque commands at 500 Hz, and low-level motor drivers track torques at over 1 kHz.

### Comparative Evaluation in Simulation
Lifting heavy unknown payloads was evaluated in the MuJoCo physics engine. Standard centroidal MPC without posture planning (non-adaptive baseline) shifted its CoM too far forward due to the added weight, failing to compensate in time and toppling forward. In contrast, the proposed method lowered its CoM in advance via optimal posture planning, and adaptive MPC immediately corrected supporting-leg torques, maintaining the CoM within stability margins throughout and completing the lift.

### Hardware Experiment 1: Static Lifting of 7 kg and 10 kg
On the real robot, cardboard box lifting tests began with 7 kg. Around 30 seconds into the run, the robot lowered its pelvis and pitched forward, smoothly transitioning into a crouch within 3 seconds. After grasping and lifting, it stood up between 55 and 80 seconds, and lowered the box back down without posture degradation.
Next, the payload was increased to 10 kg. A 10 kg payload drastically alters the robot's upper-body dynamics. At the start of the lift, slight oscillations appeared in pelvis height and pitch angle. However, the adaptive fuzzy controller quickly raised output torques to brace, stabilizing the pitch angle within seconds and returning to a full upright stance.

### Hardware Experiment 2: Locomanipulation Carrying a Payload
In a more dynamic test, the robot grasped and lifted a 7 kg payload, walked for 15 seconds (140 s to 155 s), crouched to place the box at the target location, and stood back up. Notably, the fuzzy controller parameters were not retuned at all between lifting and walking. The system demonstrated high versatility and robustness, maintaining stable bipedal walking even while carrying an unknown load.

captions.F6: Comparison of unknown payload lifting in MuJoCo. Standard centroidal MPC (left) cannot offset the added weight and topples forward (stages 1–3). The proposed method (right) coordinates posture-transition planning and adaptive torque compensation to keep its CoM low and maintain balance.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Toward practical payload-carrying humanoids
sections.summary: Integrating optimal posture planning, whole-body MPC, and adaptive fuzzy control yields robust whole-body control that resists tipping under unknown payloads. Future work aims to make fuzzy rules learning-based and improve agility.
sections.details:
This paper proposed a novel control architecture combining optimal posture-transition planning, whole-body MPC, and adaptive fuzzy control for humanoid robots handling unknown heavy payloads. Proactive trajectory optimization creates dynamically feasible reference motions, while reactive fuzzy control cancels sudden torque disturbances from unknown loads, maintaining balance without violating MPC constraints.

Extensive simulations and hardware experiments demonstrated high stability not only during static heavy-object lifting, but also during load-carrying walking (locomanipulation).

Currently, fuzzy rules are manually designed based on expert heuristics, making them somewhat reactive to rapid changes. Future work aims to optimize compensation policies using machine learning and integrate predictive disturbance observers to adapt to more agile and dynamic operational environments.

takeaways: Instead of online mass identification, applying direct torque compensation from Capture Point errors using fuzzy rules avoids transient convergence latency and parameter divergence risks.

When higher-level nonlinear MPC guarantees contact forces and CoM constraints, low-level whole-body control can track references using computationally lightweight inverse dynamics without tedious TS-QP weight tuning.
For posture transitions like crouching and standing, combining a triple-integrator (jerk minimization) with CoM stability constraints ensures smooth, jerk-free motions on real hardware.
limitations: The 125 fuzzy inference rules and membership function parameters rely on heuristic tuning based on designer experience.
Because adaptive fuzzy control is a reactive compensation scheme that acts after errors emerge, it has limits for feedforward anticipation during extremely agile motions.
Quantitative comparisons against conventional PID control have not yet been conducted and remain future work.
